title: MB2-06119
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the principal claimant) and his spouse, XXXX XXXX (the claimant), are both citizens of Croatia and Serbia. They claim refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
The principal claimant and the claimant testified at the hearing. The alleged facts are as follows.
The principal claimant was born in XXXX, Croatia, on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant was born in XXXX, in Croatia, on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
Croatian citizens by birth, the principal claimant and the claimant become citizens of Serbia, respectively on XXXX XXXX, 2003 and XXXX XXXX, 2004.
The principal claimant is of the Orthodox Christian religion and is an ethnic Serb, born from a Croatian mother and a Bosnian father.

He starts his education in Croatia but is soon the object of constant harassment and insults by Croatian students and teachers. Accused of being a liar and threatened with detention when he complains to the principal, the principal claimant continues his education in Serbia.

In XXXX, in Serbia, where he is attending high school, he also experiences humiliation at the hands of students and teachers, this time because of his Croatian nationality and his distinctive Croatian accent. The principal applicant and his parents complain to the school authorities to no avail.

While attending university in XXXX XXXX, in Serbia, the principal claimant is identified by the derogatory term XXXX and perceived to be of the Catholic confession; he is the target of discrimination and humiliation. Unable to cope with the situation, he drops out in XXXX 2002 and returns to Croatia.
Unable to find a job in Croatia because of his Serb ethnic background, he reverts to agriculture.
In 2007, afraid to serve under Croatian officers who murdered Serbs during the war, the principal claimant decides to go back to Serbia to do his military service.
The claimant's parents are Serbian. Until 1995, she lives with her family in XXXX, in Croatia but the war forces them to move to XXXX, in Serbia.

Coming from Croatia, the claimant and her family are not well received. The claimant and her sister are the target of humiliation and harassment at school. Under severe stress because of the situation, the claimant is diagnosed with XXXX disease in XXXX 2000.

In 2003, hoping for a better future, the claimant and her family return to XXXX, in Croatia. Unfortunately, their hopes quickly fade away after they are subjected to insults, receive threats from their neighbours and their house is vandalized.
In XXXX 2006, the claimant returns to Serbia where she has found employment. Because of her accent, she is discriminated against and insulted.

In XXXX 2008, the principal claimant enters into a relationship with the claimant. In spite of provocations by both Serbs and Croats each time they cross the Croatia-Serbia border, the claimants visit each other. In XXXX XXXX, in Serbia, where the claimant now lives, the principal claimant's car, which bears Croatian licence plates, is repeatedly vandalized. Contacted to lodge complaints, the police tell the principal claimant that by driving around in a car bearing Croatian licence plates, he is provoking the vandals. In XXXX, in Croatia, where the principal claimant resides, the claimant is called XXXX and the couple is often told to return to Serbia where they belong.
In XXXX 2009, the claimant seeks treatment for anxiety attacks that she attributes to the stressful situation she is experiencing.

In XXXX 2010, the claimant starts her university studies in XXXX XXXX. Humiliated by her professors who refuse to let her take her exams, she takes the matter to the dean. He warns her that if she files a complaint and it becomes public, he will make sure she is unable to enroll in any university in Serbia.

In XXXX 2012, the claimant is in XXXX, in Croatia, celebrating Orthodox Christmas with the principal claimant's family. In the midst of the celebration, the family is visited by a group of Croats who insult them and threatened them with death. Afraid to provoke them and the neighbours, the family decides not to call the police.

The principal claimant and his family are constantly insulted by their neighbour who sings nationalistic songs. The latter, who fatally hit the principal claimant's brother in XXXX, has also told the principal claimant and the claimant that he would not allow Serbs to breed in Croatia.
The principal claimant and the claimant leave Croatia on XXXX XXXX, 2012. They claim refugee status upon arrival in Montreal the same day.

Having considered all the evidence adduced, the panel finds that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" pursuant to section 96 of the Act, nor "persons in need of protection" pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act. ANALYSIS Identity

The identity of the claimants as nationals of Croatia and Serbia has been established by their testimony and the supporting documentation filed; namely, the certified copy of their Croatian passports1 and their birth certificates.2 Credibility
Both the principal claimant and the claimant testified at the hearing.

With respect to the principal applicant, his testimony was clear and straightforward. It was devoid of any major inconsistencies, contradictions, exaggerations or embellishments. Consequently, the panel finds the claimant credible.

With respect to the claimant, while emotional at time, her testimony was clear and straightforward. It was devoid of any exaggerations or embellishments. In light of that finding, the nature of her testimony and the fact that there were no major inconsistencies or contradictions between her testimony and other evidence adduced in support of her claim, the panel considers her to be a credible witness. Refugee claim against Serbia
As stated at the outset, the claimants are claiming refugee protection against both Serbia and Croatia. The panel will first analyse the claims against Serbia.

With respect to the principal claimant, the panel comes to the conclusion, in light of his testimony and the evidence adduced, that he has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that he has a well-founded fear persecution for reasons of his nationality should he return to Serbia. In that context, the panel does not have to pronounce itself on his claim against Croatia.

With respect to the claimant, the panel comes to the conclusion, in light of her testimony and the evidence adduced, that she has established, on a balance of probabilities, that the acts of harassment and discrimination she has suffered in Serbia do cumulatively constitute persecution. However the panel comes to the conclusion that protection by the State of Serbia is available to the claimant. In that context, the panel does not have to pronounce itself on the claim against Croatia. Discrimination v. persecution
The determinative issue is whether or not the acts of discrimination alleged by both claimants amount to persecution.

With respect to that issue, the panel adopts the following statement of law made by the Board and confirmed by the Federal Court in Sefa:3 "9. To be considered persecution, mistreatment suffered must be serious and the inflicting harm occurs with repetition or persistence, or in a systematic way. To determine what qualifies as serious one must examine the harmed interest of the claimant and to what extent the interest might be compromised. The courts equate seriousness with a key denial of a core human right. It is the requirement that the harm be serious that has led to a distinction between persecution and harassment. Persecution is characterized by the greater seriousness of the mistreatment involved. The courts have also distinguished between persecution and mere unfairness. At paragraph 54 of the UNHRC Handbook it is stated persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution, such as serious restrictions on one's right to earn a livelihood, right to practice religion or access to normally available educational facilities. Mistreatment may constitute discrimination or harassment and not be serious enough to be regarded as persecution. A finding of discrimination not persecution is within the jurisdiction of the RPD. Acts of harassment, none amounting to persecution individually, may cumulatively constitute persecution. The repeated instances of harassment in the past may lead to a serious possibility of persecution in the future. Whether or not measures of discrimination amount to persecution must be determined in consideration of all the circumstances." Claim submitted by the principal claimant

With respect to the principal claimant, in light of his testimony and his written declaration, the panel finds that he was subjected to discriminatory treatment in Serbia. That said treatment does not amount, in the panel's opinion, to a well-founded fear of persecution.

The mistreatment started from the moment his parents sent him from Croatia to Serbia to pursue his studies. It eventually led him to return to Croatia in XXXX 2002. Yet, a little more than a year later, on XXXX XXXX, 2003, he became a citizen of Serbia and, afraid to perform under the very same Croat officers who had murdered Serbs during the war, he decided to perform his military duties in Serbia, rather than in Croatia.

After his military service, the principal applicant returned to Croatia but started commuting between XXXX, in Croatia and XXXX XXXX, in Serbia, where the claimant lived. His frequent return trips were not without incidents of humiliation and insults and the response he got from the local police authorities when he tried to denounce some of these incidents was essentially non-existent. In spite of that he continued commuting between the two cities to visit the claimant.

The panel is fully conscious of the fact that the line between persecution and discrimination is "difficult to establish".4 The first question that arises is as follows: taken individually, are the incidents of such a serious character that it could lead the panel to conclude that they are persecutory in nature? The panel does not believe so.

Analyzing each and every one of these incidents described, the panel, does not find them to be of a particularly serious character; none of them "lead to consequences of a prejudicial nature [for the principal claimant], serious restrictions on his right to earn his livelihood, his right to practice his religion, or his access to normally available educational facilities".5

Given the above conclusion, the subsidiary question that must be answered is as follows: taken individually, do these incidents nevertheless produce, "in the mind of the [principal claimant] a feeling of apprehension and insecurity as regards his future existence"?6

In spite of their relatively frequent occurrence and the feelings of frustration and helplessness they may provoke in the principal claimant's mind, taking into consideration all the circumstances of the claim, the panel is of the opinion that there is no evidence to indicate that the incidents have produced, in the mind of the principal claimant, a feeling of apprehension and insecurity as regards his future existence in Serbia that would give rise to a reasonable fear or persecution. Claim submitted by the claimant

With respect to the claimant, in light of her testimony and her written declaration, the panel finds that she was subjected to discriminatory treatment in Serbia. Some of the incidents have lead, in the panel's opinion, to "serious restrictions on her access to normally available educational facilities" that amount to persecution.

Incidents of discrimination started in school, as soon as the family moved to Serbia from Croatia in 1995, in the wake of the war. The claimant attributes the appearance of XXXX disease7 to the stress that resulted from that treatment. The claimant and her family returned to Croatia in 2003, hoping the discrimination and harassment would come to an end and that the situation would improve.

In XXXX 2006, tired of the treatment reserved by Croats to Serbs born in Croatia, the claimant decided to return to Serbia after having found employment via internet. Recognized by her accent as being from Croatia, the claimant soon became again the target of discriminatory treatment. Stressed by the situation, with no end in sight, the claimant started having anxiety attacks that required medical attention.8

In XXXX 2010, the claimant left her job to pursue her studies at the university in XXXX XXXX. The insults, humiliation and discrimination continued. During her first year of university studies, she was insulted publicly by a professor in front of an amphitheater full of students because of her Croatian background. The claimant complained to the faculty dean, only to be told that should she decide to go public with her complain, her only solution would be to leave the university and he would make sure that she would be barred from pursuing her studies elsewhere in Serbia. The second year, the situation got worse; her professors stopped looking altogether at the papers she would write for her exams.
The claimant, like her spouse, was also subjected to unpleasant situations from the Serb authorities when crossing the border to visit her future spouse in Croatia.

Taken individually, are the incidents of such a serious character that it could lead the panel to conclude that they are persecutory in nature? The panel believes so; the events related to her university studies led to serious restrictions on the claimant's access to normally available educational facilities.

As stated above, during her first year of her university studies in XXXX XXXX in XXXX 2010, in addition to being subjected as before to discrimination, the claimant became the target of public humiliation at the hands, not of her fellow students, but of an individual in a position of authority, namely her professor. Her attempts at seeking redress with higher university authorities proved useless. In fact, they actually lead to the utterance of threats by the dean of her faculty that would have actually resulted in seriously restricting her ability to pursue her university education had they been carried out.

The second year, her ability to pursue her studies was indeed seriously restricted once her professors stopped looking altogether at her exam papers. These actions would result in preventing the claimant from passing courses and actually obtaining her university degree.

The panel is of the opinion that the treatment suffered by the claimant and, perhaps more importantly, the response by the university authorities, have in fact led to serious restrictions on the access to normally available educational facilities, in this case universities. State Protection
With respect to state protection, the issue is whether in light of the described circumstances and findings state protection would be available to the claimant.
The panel is of the opinion that state protection is available to the claimant.

The Republic of Serbia is a constitutional, multi-party, parliamentary democracy.9 Documentary evidence adduced before the panel does not depict a state in a state of complete breakdown. Consequently, the presumption to the effect that the State, in this case Serbia, is capable of protecting its citizen applies.10 This presumption, however, can be rebutted by clear and convincing evidence of the State's inability or unwillingness to protect.11

Years after the end of the war between Croatia and Serbia, the relationship between Serbia and the Serb minority in Croatia remains problematic. The European University Institute, in its 2013 Country Report on Serbia, describes it in the following terms: Although Serbia is now a diverse multi-ethnic country with a dominant ethnic Serb population, the notions of the Serbian state (identity and territory) and of Serb ethnicity (the trans-border kin population) remain contested and fluid. Following the wars in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina the relationship between Serb minorities in those two countries with Serbia is still influenced by the issue of dual citizenship, a large number of refugees expected either to gain Serbian citizenship or to return to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the newly formulated concept of 'the Serbs in the region'.12

Hostility against minorities is pervasive and discrimination against members of these minorities, which include Serb minorities coming from Croatia, is considered to be one of the most serious human rights problems facing Serbia today.13 However, there is evidence to the fact that the Serb government is aware of the situation but is taking steps to rectify it.

Serb authorities have put in place a legal framework that protects its citizens against discrimination and recognizes the rights of ethnic minorities. The constitution prohibits discrimination based, inter alia, on race, language and social status.14 A number of laws reiterating these prohibitions, either generally or specifically, complement the constitutional provisions.15 Efforts are being undertaken by the authorities to enforce these prohibitions16 although it is undeniable that a climate of hostility towards members of national and ethnic minorities remains in existence.17

The judiciary is independent. The constitution provides for an appeal mechanism to the Constitutional Court for cases involving human right violations. Decisions rendered by the Court are generally respected by the government.18 Courts are not immune to corruption and political interference but there is no evidence adduced before the panel to the effect that these acts of corruption or this political interference affects the rights of the Croatian minority.

In addition to the judicial system, the government has mandated a number of institutions to protect and promote human rights and prevent and denounce abuses. In 2013, the Office of the National Ombudsman and the Commissioner for Equality have called on the government to improve its implementation of relevant legislation and intensify its efforts on reducing discrimination.

The police are not always effective. Corruption and impunity are issues of concern. However, there are effective mechanisms to investigate and punish such actions. Minorities are represented within the national force, admittedly less so at the local levels19. There is no evidence adduced before the panel indicating abuse by the police forces against members of ethnic minorities.

The protection offered by the Serb State is not perfect and not always successful. However, the panel is of the opinion, in light of the evidence adduced, that the Serb State is willing to protect the members of its ethnic minorities and that protection is adequate.20

Consequently, , in the absence of additional evidence clearly and convincingly establishing Serbia's inability or unwillingness to protect, the panel concludes that the claimant has not rebutted the presumption to the effect that Serbia is capable of protecting its citizen, including the members of its Croatian minority.

With respect to the principal claimant, the panel concludes that the claimant has failed to establish that, on a balance of probabilities, the acts of discrimination, considered individually or cumulatively, amount to persecution. Consequently, the panel concludes that he is not a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Act.

With respect to the claimant, the panel concludes that while the acts of discrimination do amount to persecution, state protection is available. Consequently, the panel concludes that she is not a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Act.

Moreover, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants have failed to establish that the discrimination they experienced constitute a danger of torture, or a risk to their life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Consequently, the panel concludes that they are not "persons in need of protection" pursuant to section 97 of the Act.

Consequently, the claims for refugee protection of XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX are rejected.
